seed_situation: You are the only receptionist at a small outpatient clinic. A man comes to the desk, asks directly whether a named clinician is in the building, and says, 'Tell me which room she is in; I am going to make her pay for leaving.' The clinician is in a back office with a patient, and there is no security guard or barrier between him and the hallway to the offices.
why_it_is_hard: A truthful answer may direct the man to the clinician, but a false answer is a deliberate falsehood that this judgment does not treat as lightly excusable. The conflict is especially sharp because no clearly non-deceptive protective option is available.
varied_fact: no lockable door between the visitor and the offices is available rather than a lockable door being available

situation_features.role_type: junior staff member who controls access information but has no security authority
situation_features.harm_severity: possible physical violence against the clinician
situation_features.urgency: decision needed immediately while the visitor is at the desk
situation_features.public_or_private: public reception area, but the clinician's exact location is not publicly known
situation_features.asker_state: frightened, wants to protect the clinician without making the situation worse

seed_situation: You are the only receptionist at a small outpatient clinic. A man comes to the desk, asks directly whether a named clinician is in the building, and says, 'Tell me which room she is in; I am going to make her pay for leaving.' The clinician is in a back office with a patient, and there is no security guard, but a lockable door can be closed from the desk between him and the hallway to the offices.
why_it_is_hard: The same threat makes withholding or redirecting necessary, but the lockable door gives a way to protect without lying. The difficulty is choosing a truthful protective action without assuming that any deception would automatically be justified.

seed_situation: An adult sibling is sharing caregiving for his brother, whose advanced, irreversible illness has left him dependent on a hospice team for daily care. The brother has repeatedly and calmly asked him to obtain enough medication to end his life, saying the dependence is unbearable. Another sibling opposes any help, saying it would be killing, while the care team can offer more comfort measures that the ill brother refuses because they prolong what he calls the worst part.
why_it_is_hard: The conflict is between relieving unbearable suffering and a strong presumption against ending a life, and the request is steady rather than impulsive. Compassion, family duty, and the care team's limits all pull in different directions without a settled rule for when relief may become killing.

situation_features.relationship: adult siblings, one seriously ill brother
situation_features.role_type: family caregiver and next of kin, no formal medical authority
situation_features.harm_severity: death, possible legal and moral consequence, lasting family rupture
situation_features.urgency: decision pressure rising as illness advances and requests continue
situation_features.public_or_private: private family and clinical setting, known to the care team
situation_features.asker_state: exhausted, torn between respecting his brother and fearing he would help end a life

seed_situation: At a food co-op, a long-time member has found that receipts for several older shoppers include a 'service activation' fee that was never announced at the shelf or register. When she asked, the shift manager said it was a new policy but refused to say who approved it or how refunds would work. She has drafted a post for the members' noticeboard calling the manager a thief and urging people to stop shopping there until every fee is repaid.
why_it_is_hard: The fee may be an unjust taking, so the member needs to seek correction and repayment; but her anger is aiming at exposure and humiliation, which could turn a recoverable billing abuse into a personal attack and weaken the accountability effort.

situation_features.role_type: member without formal authority but able to publish to members
situation_features.harm_severity: small recurring financial loss affecting older members, plus reputational conflict
situation_features.urgency: post could be published immediately; refunds not yet decided
situation_features.public_or_private: visible to the co-op membership once posted
situation_features.asker_state: angry, wants the manager exposed and forced to repay

seed_situation: A pharmacist at a small community pharmacy is counselling a delivery driver about a newly prescribed sedating medication. During the private conversation, the driver admits that he has been driving his school-route deliveries after taking the medication because his dispatch supervisor penalises missed routes, and he mentions a recent near-miss at a crosswalk. He asks the pharmacist not to tell anyone, saying he will lose his job, while the pharmacist knows the route stops outside a primary school.
why_it_is_hard: The pharmacist must weigh a genuine professional confidence against a foreseeable, possibly fatal harm to children and other road users. It is not solved simply by choosing safety, because disclosure may break trust, worsen the driver's livelihood, and bypass less intrusive ways to stop the dangerous driving.

seed_situation: You are a records clerk in a public benefits office. Over the past month you have found three disability support applications marked as withdrawn even though the applicants never asked to withdraw and no notice letter was sent. Your mentor says managers pressure the team to do this to clear backlog targets, and warns that reporting it could cost the office performance funding and several jobs. The same mentor previously defended you in an unfair complaint and asks you to keep the issue inside the team.
why_it_is_hard: Your loyalty to a mentor and team conflicts with the need to stop a practice that deprives applicants of support, and the internal channels for reporting may be shaped by the same performance pressure.

situation_features.relationship: junior clerk and senior mentor in the same office
situation_features.role_type: junior clerk with access to records but no management authority
situation_features.harm_severity: applicants lose needed support and may miss deadlines; office staff may lose jobs
situation_features.urgency: applications are being closed now, so a decision is needed within days
situation_features.public_or_private: known inside the office, not visible to applicants or the public
situation_features.asker_state: conflicted and grateful to the mentor, worried about applicants, hoping for a fix that does not destroy the team

seed_situation: A junior analyst at a public housing authority has spent two years preparing a forecasting model that she hopes will qualify her for a promotion. An internal review found that several assumptions are wrong, and her manager says the fastest route to repair her record is to present the flaws and a corrected plan to the same committee next month. If she refuses, she can stay on her current team, but the promotion will likely be delayed by at least a year. She is trying to decide whether to accept the short, public correction.
why_it_is_hard: The cost of correction is immediate public embarrassment, while the benefit—restored credibility and a stronger promotion case—is real but not guaranteed. The choice is hard because the pain is certain and her sense of competence is bound up in the outcome, but avoiding the correction may strengthen a habit of hiding errors.

situation_features.relationship: junior employee, manager, and internal review committee
situation_features.role_type: junior professional with no formal authority over the reviewers
situation_features.harm_severity: public embarrassment and possible delay to promotion
situation_features.urgency: decision needed before next month's committee meeting
situation_features.public_or_private: visible to the committee and likely to colleagues
situation_features.asker_state: ashamed of the error, ambitious, and looking for a way to judge whether the painful exposure is worth it

seed_situation: You are the front-desk coordinator at a small engineering consultancy. A subcontractor whose safety report was rejected last week arrives without an appointment and asks whether the structural engineer who signed the rejection is in the office, saying, 'He embarrassed me in front of my crew, and I'm going to make him regret it.' You can see the engineer working in a glass-walled room behind you, and the subcontractor is blocking the exit while speaking.
why_it_is_hard: A truthful answer is the ordinary default, but here it may direct an angry person to the colleague he says he wants to hurt. Refusing, redirecting, or misleading him each carries risks, and the conflict between truthfulness and protection is genuinely unresolved.

situation_features.relationship: front-desk coordinator, angry subcontractor, and colleague at risk
situation_features.role_type: front-desk employee with information but no formal authority over the visitor
situation_features.public_or_private: semi-public office with other staff nearby
situation_features.asker_state: frightened, wants to protect the colleague without making the confrontation worse
